title: Game Jam Sidekick
user: A programming parent helping an 8–13-year-old turn their own art and game ideas into one small playable project each week.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Parent says their child wants to make games; they use Scratch and GameMaker but need a fun path through the many skills.
A teacher reports students cannot export Song Maker work as MIDI on Chromebooks, showing the handoff from playful creation to reuse is fragile.

recurrence: Two 2025 HN parent threads plus recurring classroom export reports; severity is high because the adult must continually invent the next achievable task.
current_workaround: Parents stitch together Scratch tutorials, art prompts, and a weekly video call or sit beside the child.
incumbents_and_gap: Scratch, GameMaker and Phaser tutorials teach tools; none supplies an adult-child, asset-first game-jam ritual with a tiny finish line.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with 20 printable/on-screen prompt cards, a three-step idea→asset→play loop, local project gallery, and a shareable completed-game postcard. Non-goals: code editor, hosted games, AI generation, curriculum management.
success_measure: 30% of first-week households save two completed project postcards within 14 days.
monetization: one-time — parents can buy a durable set of fresh prompts without a child-data subscription.
constraints: No accounts or child profiling; COPPA-aware copy; local storage only; accessible keyboard and touch flow.
why_distinct: It is a facilitation tool for co-making, not another programming course or game engine.

title: Takebook
user: Music teachers and pairs practicing a short piano phrase together who need to keep, annotate, and reopen takes without a DAW.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An adult teaching an 11-year-old is advised to favor browser-based, instant-feedback projects; a reply describes making a game together to keep learning concrete.
A Shared Piano teacher uses it daily and explicitly asks to export MIDI into Logic and other DAWs.

recurrence: The same browser-first, instant-feedback need appears in current parent discussion and a teacher’s daily-use feature request.
current_workaround: Use Shared Piano then screen-record, download files manually, or move to a full DAW.
incumbents_and_gap: Chrome Music Lab is playful and Logic is powerful; neither is a lightweight practice takebook with phrase notes and one-click MIDI/WAV handoff.
smallest_useful_product: Web MIDI piano-roll recorder: record up to 60 seconds, loop a marked bar range, attach a teacher note, and export standard MIDI/WAV. Non-goals: notation engraving, collaboration server, licensed sounds.
success_measure: At least 40% of activated users export or reopen a saved take in the same week.
monetization: freemium — free local takes; a low-cost teacher pack can add folders and printable practice sheets.
constraints: Web MIDI support varies; must function with computer keyboard; no recording upload by default; generated audio uses own synth samples.
why_distinct: A take-and-feedback utility, not a generic online piano or a DAW clone.

title: MoveMap
user: Webcam-motion game makers and players who need to test whether a body gesture can be recognized reliably in a real room before mapping it to a game action.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A maker describes a universal MediaPipe/OpenCV webcam controller mapping gestures to keypresses without VR hardware; commenters question practical targeting and control precision.
An OBS virtual-camera user reports it still occupies the system camera after uninstall, a concrete reason to avoid install-level camera plumbing for playful tools.

recurrence: Gesture control repeatedly reaches the calibration problem; installation and camera conflicts make experimentation disproportionately costly.
current_workaround: Write one-off MediaPipe scripts, tweak thresholds in source, and install virtual-camera or input-emulation software.
incumbents_and_gap: MediaPipe provides landmarks and Kinect-style projects provide demos; neither gives a local browser test bench that explains false positives and exports a portable gesture profile.
smallest_useful_product: Local browser app: define 1–3 pose checkpoints, collect 10 examples, show live confidence/history, and export a JSON threshold profile. Non-goals: OS key injection, surveillance, cloud video storage, multiplayer game engine.
success_measure: 60% of sessions complete a calibration and replay a 30-second test without a false trigger reported by the user.
monetization: one-time — a maker utility has episodic, project-based use.
constraints: On-device camera processing only; clear consent indicator; accessibility warning that movement is optional; no biometric identity inference.
why_distinct: It validates and communicates gesture reliability rather than pretending to be a universal controller.

title: Together Room
user: A parent and child who want a 10-minute remote co-op activity without ads, logins, tracking, or an ongoing game-service commitment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A father seeking remote co-op with a 10-year-old reports hours of searching through dark patterns, data harvesting, recurring fees, and unreliable services.
A Godot user reports that exporting a project breaks multiplayer, illustrating why small family games often fail outside the developer’s machine.

recurrence: The HN request is explicit and severe; remote co-op reliability is a known deployment burden even in mainstream game tooling.
current_workaround: Search app stores, tolerate ads/permissions, or persuade a technically skilled parent to host a game.
incumbents_and_gap: Roblox, mobile F2P games and Discord activities optimize retention or accounts; the gap is a calm, invite-link-only two-person activity.
smallest_useful_product: A two-device PWA with three original, turn-based co-op microgames, six-digit room codes, reconnect support, and no account. Non-goals: open chat, UGC, matchmaking, payments by children.
success_measure: 50% of created rooms complete two rounds with both devices still connected after 10 minutes.
monetization: one-time — a transparent family purchase directly addresses subscription fatigue.
constraints: No ads, analytics minimization, original game content only, safety-first room expiry, COPPA-aware product design.
why_distinct: A deliberately bounded family activity room, not a social gaming platform.

title: TickLens
user: Indie browser-game developers trying to find why room updates lag long before CPU appears saturated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Node/Socket.IO game developer sees lag at 500 players despite low CPU; replies point to I/O throughput and accidentally quadratic outbound updates.
A multiplayer user needs separate server/client paths and encounters authority errors, showing that state topology becomes hard to see as games grow.

recurrence: A current production-scale report and ongoing engine-level multiplayer complexity point to a visibility gap rather than a mere framework choice.
current_workaround: Add ad-hoc logs, inspect CPU dashboards, or guess at Socket.IO traffic patterns.
incumbents_and_gap: Datadog and OpenTelemetry are infrastructure-first; game engines expose state but do not make per-room fanout and tick cost legible.
smallest_useful_product: Drop-in JS client/server probe that records tick duration, room size, bytes/messages per room, and emits a self-contained HTML trace. Non-goals: hosting, matchmaking, packet capture, engine lock-in.
success_measure: In a seeded 500-client test, users identify the highest fanout room from the report in under five minutes.
monetization: freemium — open local reports build trust; paid team retention/compare reports can fund it.
constraints: No payload capture by default; redact IDs; overhead budget under 2%; Socket.IO/WebSocket adapters initially only.
why_distinct: It diagnoses game-state fanout, not generic server performance.

title: Replay Capsule
user: A solo developer of a 2D browser game who needs a bug report that recreates the player’s inputs and timing without operating a full analytics stack.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer asks what people use besides Phaser for multiplayer 2D browser games, signaling continued fragmentation in the browser-game stack.
A canvas user hits an export limit despite having relatively few objects; canvas projects need bounded, portable artifacts rather than ever-larger captures.

recurrence: Browser-game makers repeatedly assemble their own stack, while canvas export limits show the need to cap diagnostic artifacts from day one.
current_workaround: Ask for a screen recording, add console logs, or attempt to reproduce a vague report manually.
incumbents_and_gap: Sentry replays general web sessions and engine tooling is engine-specific; neither offers a tiny deterministic input-and-seed capsule for plain canvas games.
smallest_useful_product: NPM library to record pointer/key/gamepad events plus developer-supplied seed and checkpoints, then download/import a capped replay file. Non-goals: video recording, user-session tracking, server playback, anti-cheat.
success_measure: A sample Phaser/Kaplay demo reproduces 90% of seeded failures from a single imported capsule.
monetization: free — adoption depends on trust and easy inclusion in small open-source games.
constraints: Explicit opt-in UI; never record text fields; strict size cap; browser API compatibility and gamepad timestamp caveats.
why_distinct: It is an event-level reproducibility primitive, not surveillance replay or a game framework.

title: Patchboard
user: Creative coders learning Web Audio who need to hear and inspect a small signal graph before embedding it in a performance or toy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An HN maker asks what is hardest about Web Audio after building a graph visualizer, identifying exploration and debugging as the problem space.
A Tone.js user reports Player audio falling out of sync with Transport timers under common timing changes.

recurrence: Graph comprehension and timing correctness remain separate pain points for browser-audio makers.
current_workaround: Read API docs, make throwaway CodePens, or debug by ear in an application that also contains UI and game logic.
incumbents_and_gap: Tone.js is a programming library and DAWs are heavyweight; neither is a local, inspectable micro-patch notebook with timing probes.
smallest_useful_product: Static web patchboard with six native nodes, animated signal path, BPM scheduler, click-to-hear A/B changes, and shareable URL fragment. Non-goals: DAW tracks, cloud projects, sample marketplace, AI composition.
success_measure: At least 35% of first sessions save or share a patch after changing three graph connections.
monetization: free — educational utility and organic sharing are more valuable than gating a small learning tool.
constraints: Use only synthesized sound; reduce-motion option; autoplay requires a user gesture; no microphone permission in v1.
why_distinct: It teaches audible causal relationships in a graph, rather than wrapping an LLM around sound design.

title: RAW Recipe Cards
user: Beginning photographers who want deliberate, repeatable RAW-edit practice instead of copying opaque presets.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A photographer explicitly asks how to get good at RAW editing after learning that familiar image looks arise from specific processing choices.
A darktable Color-EQ report describes interactive picker failures, showing how manipulating a rich editor can distract from learning a visual adjustment.

recurrence: The learning question is direct and the major free RAW workflow’s history complexity confirms the gap between editing and explaining edits.
current_workaround: Buy presets, watch long videos, or inspect a long slider/history stack without knowing what to try next.
incumbents_and_gap: Lightroom presets and darktable history show results and operations; neither gives a constrained visual drill with a reason for each move.
smallest_useful_product: Offline web simulator using licensed Creative Commons practice images: five cards such as recover sky or shape color, three exposed controls, before/after and reflection note. Non-goals: RAW decoding, photo hosting, presets marketplace, AI enhancement.
success_measure: 40% of users complete three cards and revisit one within seven days.
monetization: one-time — a compact practice deck is understandable and avoids subscription pressure on learners.
constraints: Use only owned/CC images; disclose that it is a learning simulator rather than a camera-RAW processor; keyboard-accessible controls.
why_distinct: It turns processing knowledge into practice, not another preset pack or editor.

title: Continuity Board
user: Tabletop groups and hobby comic makers who need to keep character appearance, props, and panel intent consistent across a short story.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A player wants consistent character drawings and panels from an RPG campaign, reporting that models tried do not keep consistency.
An Excalidraw issue asks for a more navigable export workflow, reinforcing that an idea board must hand off cleanly to a final artifact.

recurrence: Character continuity is a specific request; makers also struggle to turn an infinite canvas into a usable export.
current_workaround: Keep folders of reference images, retype long prompts, or make a giant whiteboard and manually crop it.
incumbents_and_gap: Miro/Excalidraw are generic canvases and image generators make images; neither has structured character locks and shot cards without generating copyrighted-style output.
smallest_useful_product: Local board with character reference slots, named attributes, prop checklist, 4–12 panel shot cards, and print/PDF export. Non-goals: image generation, style imitation, public galleries, collaborative server.
success_measure: 50% of new boards export a 4-panel sheet with every panel linked to at least one reference card.
monetization: one-time — hobby projects benefit from a durable ownership model.
constraints: Local files by default; no copyrighted character templates; clearly label user-created references; PDF export must preserve attribution fields.
why_distinct: It addresses continuity before art is made, avoiding a thin generative-comic wrapper.

title: Demo Loop
user: Creative-technology students needing a credible 20–45 second proof-of-interaction for a portfolio, even when their prototype is fragile.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A creative-technology student says portfolio projects matter at least as much as coding skill when pursuing internships.
A browser-audio maker reports Recorder behavior on Chrome, illustrating how even small interactive demos need reliable capture rather than a live-only presentation.

recurrence: Portfolio pressure is current, and browser demos regularly encounter capture reliability problems.
current_workaround: Screen-record many takes with OS tools, trim in a video editor, or show a fragile live link.
incumbents_and_gap: Loom and OBS are general recording tools; they do not frame a compact interaction demo with input, caption, and fallback still in one artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Browser recorder that captures a selected tab plus optional mic, lets the maker mark one interaction beat and one caption, and exports a short WebM and poster image. Non-goals: cloud hosting, multi-track editing, analytics, AI video generation.
success_measure: 60% of recordings are exported without opening another editor.
monetization: one-time — students value an affordable portfolio utility more than another subscription.
constraints: Use screen-capture permission only on explicit action; keep media local; browser codec fallbacks; never claim archival quality.
why_distinct: It is tuned to showing an interaction’s cause and effect, not a generic screencast service.

title: Motion Feel Lab
user: Indie animators and game/UI makers trying to turn a desired feeling—hesitation, weight, anticipation—into an editable motion curve.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A researcher asks about optimizing aesthetic, non-uniform movement because basic kinematic/pathing models do not express desired qualities.
A composer asks for offline rendering because recording a generated result in real time produces an unusable fast file; creative timing needs inspectable, deterministic output.

recurrence: Creators struggle both to specify expressive timing and to faithfully render it for comparison.
current_workaround: Tweak Bezier handles blind, search easing cheat sheets, or keyframe in a full animation package.
incumbents_and_gap: cubic-bezier.com visualizes curves and full animation apps keyframe scenes; neither starts from motion intent and compares the same move side by side.
smallest_useful_product: Static playground with six motion intents, editable position/rotation curves, onion-path preview, 2/4/8-frame comparison, and CSS/JS export. Non-goals: character rigging, physics simulation, generative animation, video export.
success_measure: 35% of sessions export a curve after comparing at least two variants.
monetization: free — shareable outputs and search discovery suit a small focused reference utility.
constraints: Reduced-motion mode; frame-rate-independent preview; use descriptive labels without claiming universal emotional meaning.
why_distinct: It makes timing a deliberate creative decision, not an AI animation generator.

title: Postcard FX
user: Friends and event hosts wanting a playful, phone-first face effect that produces a shareable still without installing a virtual camera or surrendering video to a service.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A webcam laser-eyes toy earned positive response, but a mobile user reports portrait output is vertically squashed—the quick prototype misses real phone capture needs.
OBS users report macOS code-signing failure when installing virtual-camera support, a concrete friction point for camera-effect experiments.

recurrence: Playful webcam effects attract interest, while phone orientation and virtual-camera installation create immediate adoption failures.
current_workaround: Use social-network filters, awkward desktop webcam sites, or install OBS/virtual-camera components.
incumbents_and_gap: Snapchat and Instagram filters are platform-bound; OBS virtual camera is heavyweight. The gap is a private, browser-native postcard effect.
smallest_useful_product: Phone-first local web app with face landmarks, three original geometric effects, portrait-safe crop guides, timer, and PNG download. Non-goals: social feed, face recognition, video storage, branded celebrity effects.
success_measure: 70% of permission-granting mobile users reach a downloaded PNG within two minutes.
monetization: free — lightweight shareability is the distribution mechanism; no need to monetize biometric-adjacent play.
constraints: Process camera frames on device; never identify faces; explicit permission and deletion language; support no-camera preview mode.
why_distinct: It is a privacy-preserving, orientation-correct camera toy—not another social filter network.
